catalog_quote: [p. 253] The stem of the second-person dual, PK *nhula, is probably related to PPN *NHuNpalV by syncope of the unstressed syllable (stress at all stages of Karnic is on the initial syllable of the word); clearly is it more likely that this change happened once, in a language which was ancestral to all Karnic languages, than individually, in each daughter language. ... [p. 248, Table 1: Languages and sources] Language and dialects | Major sources | Abbrev. ... Mithaka | Breen n.d. b | Mith ... [p. 248, fn. 15] Languages names ' bold are Karnic. All figures are percentages. Note that some of these figures may be revised when (and if) more accurate data become available. For example, because of gaps in the data, the list for Mithaka contains only 66 items, and these percentages are therefore obviously less accurate than those between well-attested languages.

File (18 pp., the PDF's metadata gives the title 'Karnic classification revisited', author Claire Bowern; PL-512:245-262, DOI 10.15144/PL-512.245, CC BY-SA 2015 online edition). PDF page 9 = printed p. 253 (running head 'Karnic classification revisited 253'). extracted text of that page gives, word for word: 'The stem of the second-person dual, PK *nhula, is probably related to PPN *NHuNpalV by syncope of the unstressed syllable (stress at all stages of Karnic is on the initial syllable of the word); clearly is it more likely that this change happened once, in a language which was ancestral to all Karnic languages, than individually, in each daughter languag…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Family-level statement only: in Karnic languages (Bowern's sample includes Mithaka) word stress falls on the initial syllable. No source opened gives a Mithaka-specific stress rule; Breen 1997 pp. 79-80, the only first-hand published phonological remarks on Mithaka, describe stops and rhotics and are silent on stress.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not mentioned for Mithaka. (Breen 2004 §3.6 for the closely related Yandruwandha: secondary stress on the third syllable of four-syllable roots and on bound disyllabic morphemes; Breen 1997 p. 79 says Mithaka 'seems to be rather similar in phonology to Yandruwandha', but that remark concerns segments, not stress.)
new_statements.domain_note: Bowern's remark is a parenthetical in a comparative reconstruction of pronouns, made about Karnic as a whole ('at all stages of Karnic'), i.e. word-level initial stress; it is not based on a stated analysis of the Mithaka recordings (Breen's fieldnotes, cited as her Mithaka source, are unpublished and her Mithaka list has only 66 items).
new_statements.identity_note: Mithaka (mith1236) = AUSTLANG L34 Midhaga/Mithaka; speakers Bill Gorringe and Maudie Naylon called it Marrula / Marrunada (Breen 1971 p. 9). Glottolog groups it with Karuwali (karr1236, AUSTLANG L35) under 'Mithaka-Karuwali' (mith1235); Nash 2025 says Karuwali 'is nowadays subsumed under the name Mithaka as recorded by Breen (1968-70)'. The Campbell 1899 'Murunuda' wordlist in Mathew's Eaglehawk and Crow is the Marrunada variety of Mithaka. Bowern 2001 p. 253 statement is about Karnic as a whole, not a specific Mithaka dialect.

sources.note: The only published first-hand phonological remarks on Mithaka (pp. 79-80): 'Mithaka, in which I have a few hours of fairly poor quality recording from two informants, seems to be rather similar in phonology to Yandruwandha: it has a voicing distinction in perhaps all stop positions, apico-alveolar and retroflex trill-released stops.. and the usual trill, tap and glide.' Transcriptions 'preliminary and tentative'. Nothing on Mithaka stress; the paper's stress remarks (after 'primary stressed (first) vowel') concern Pitta-Pitta, Alyawarr, Wambaya, Djapu.

sources.note: Silent on stress. Section 15-6 'Mitaka' (p. 9) says the writer recorded 'a medium corpus' from Bill Gorringe (who calls the language Marrula / Marrunada) and Maudie Naylon of Birdsville; pp. 23-24 give a present-tense auxiliary example (nanji kulinde kuli 'I am sitting') and note a voiced/voiceless apical stop contrast shared with the Karna chain. Lexicostatistic classification and wordlists only; the words 'stress' and 'accent' do not occur in the text.
